prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and biology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, but I want the case to rest on merit rather than on that unanimity. It is one of the few arcs in medicine that runs unbroken from peptide biochemistry (proglucagon processing, the truncated active GLP-1(7-36) amide, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, satiety and glucagonostatic actions) to drugs with proven benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The basic findings are 30 to 40 years old, large independent randomised outcome trials have confirmed them, and the therapeutic class is stable and still expanding. A physiology-focused prize to Holst, Drucker and Mojsov honours the discovery step, which is where the Nobel tradition has usually placed credit, and keeps the configuration at three.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The medicines that changed care (liraglutide, semaglutide) depend on Knudsen's acylation and half-life engineering, and a prize that omits her can be read as honouring the hormone and not the therapy. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener's group, which is not on the supplied list, cannot be settled from the files in front of us, and a three-person cap forces an exclusion in either direction. If the committee judges that the drug-development arm is the heart of the achievement, my preferred trio is the wrong one. A secondary concern is that this is the obvious choice, and obviousness should not stand in for scrutiny of the credit.

responses.point: Sandberg backs GLP-1 first but treats Mojsov's identification of the bioactive peptide as decisive yet contested, and regards Knudsen's work as drug design rather than discovery.
responses.response: I share the concern about Mojsov and agree it cannot be resolved from the supplied text, which is why I do not present her inclusion as secure. I would qualify the discovery versus drug design line, though. Pharmaceutical engineering that makes a native peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly drug is a scientific achievement and not routine development. I keep Knudsen out because three places force a choice and the physiology claims are the more standard basis for credit, not because her contribution is lesser. If colleagues think the therapeutic arm carries the prize, I am open to replacing one of the three, and Mojsov is where I would hesitate most.

responses.point: El Manira ranks optogenetics (B012) second and acknowledges that six credited names exceed the three-person cap, so any trio such as Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel excludes deserving people.
responses.response: I agree that optogenetics is a major methodological advance, but I would not make it the second item in a combined prize. The credit problem you describe is more severe than for GLP-1: Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck each have a real claim, and the trio you propose rests on a judgement that neuronal deployment and channel discovery carry equal weight. A tool is a different kind of achievement from a therapy that changes disease outcomes, and the two do not naturally pair under one citation. If we wanted a second part, a two-person immunology or cell-biology achievement with a clean credit would split the three places more sensibly. I would still place B012 behind B010 and B017 on clarity of attribution.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (B051, Walter and Mori) third and sees a clean two-person attribution and a pathway now central to protein homeostasis.
responses.response: I accept that the attribution for Walter and Mori is cleaner than for most candidates and that the mechanism is textbook. My hesitation is on the medicine side of our remit: Ron's PERK arm and the later ATF6 branch are acknowledged as gaps, and clinical translation is still early, so the case for medicine rests on relevance to disease and not on demonstrated benefit. I would not rank it above TNF blockade or CAR-T, where the discovery has already changed outcomes for large patient groups. I would not oppose it as a later pairing, but I do not see why it should displace those two.

responses.point: Linnarsson places CAR-T second and antisense correction of SMN2 (B040) fourth, noting that foundational CAR priority (Eshhar and others) remains open.
responses.response: I agree that CAR-T is the strongest challenger after GLP-1, and I ranked it third. The open question of the original chimeric receptor concept is real and affects whether June, Sadelain and Rosenberg is the right set. Rosenberg's case is stronger for adoptive cell transfer than for CAR design itself, as Sandberg notes. On SMN2, I agree the mechanism-to-drug story is very clean, but I rank it lower than you do because the platform is younger and the long-term durability data are still accumulating. I would revisit it in a few years rather than now.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide can be separated from Habener's group, which is not on the credited list.
Whether the committee prefers to credit physiology (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) or the drug-development arm (Knudsen) when only three places are available.
For TNF blockade (B010), whether the committee regards the contributions of antibody engineers and TNF cloners as outside the core credit.
For CAR-T (B017), whether Eshhar's early receptor work should alter the credited set.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration. My field of experimental rheumatology means I have subject expertise in TNF blockade (B010), which I list as an alternative, but I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Feldmann or Maini. My recorded co-authors (Kuchroo, Sonesson) and my Bergen affiliation do not connect me to any shortlisted candidate, and I do not infer ties from shared institutions.
